## Introduction

### Overview

This page contains additional plotting material that builds on
the [week 13 data visualization lecture](../week13/w13b_data-viz.qmd),
and covers the following topics:

- [Setting a default theme](#setting-a-default-theme-with-theme_set) ---
  Using `theme_set()` to give all plots the same look.
- [Adjusting axes with `scale_` functions](#adjusting-axes-with-scale_-functions) ---
  Number formatting, axis limits, tick marks, and axis expansion.
- [Bar graphs with `geom_bar()`](#bar-graphs-with-geom_bar) and [histograms](#histograms)
- [Faceting](#faceting) --- Splitting a plot into multiple panels.
- [Customizing themes](#customizing-themes) and [color palettes](#color-palettes)
- [Combining plots into one figure](#combining-plots-into-one-figure) --- Using the _patchwork_ package.

### Setting up

1. Open Positron and connect to OSC with your personal dir open,
   like in the [w12b lecture](/week12/w12b_r-basics.qmd#setup-starting-positron-and-connecting-to-osc).
2. Open your `week13` folder in Positron,
   and create a new Quarto document `bonus_plotting.qmd` in it, with a YAML header.
3. Run the examples and exercises in code chunks in this document.

### Packages and data

This page uses the same package and data as in week 13.
Load the _tidyverse_, which includes _ggplot2_:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
```
:::


Read the count table and the metadata:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
counts <- read_tsv(
  "/fs/ess/PAS3493/share/week13/salmon.merged.gene_counts_length_scaled.tsv"
)
meta <- read_tsv("../garrigos/meta/metadata.tsv")
```
:::



::: {.cell}

:::


Make a count table with the metadata added,
and per-sample summaries of library size and number of detected genes:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Make a long-format count table with the metadata added:
counts_long <- counts |>
  select(!gene_name) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = !gene_id, names_to = "sample_id", values_to = "count") |>
  left_join(meta, by = "sample_id") |>
  # Make time a factor so that 24 hpi comes first:
  mutate(time = factor(time, levels = c("24hpi", "10dpi")))

# Compute library size and number of detected genes per sample:
sample_stats <- counts_long |>
  summarize(
    lib_size_M = sum(count) / 1e6,
    n_detected = sum(count > 0),
    .by = c(sample_id, treatment, time)
  )
```
:::


## Setting a default theme with `theme_set()`

In the [week 13 lecture](../week13/w13b_data-viz.qmd#adding-labels-and-a-theme),
you added a theme like `theme_bw()` to individual plots.
When you want all the plots you produce in (e.g.) a Quarto document to have the
same look, you can instead set a **default theme** with `theme_set()`.

For example, to use `theme_bw()` throughout:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
theme_set(theme_bw())
```
:::


You can also add customization to the persistent theme with `theme()`
(more on this function [below](#customizing-themes)), for example:

- Use a larger text and point size for all plots (increased `base_size`)
- Remove the minor grid lines (`panel.grid.minor`)
- Center (rather than left-align) the title (`plot.title`)


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
theme_set(
  # base_size sets the size of all text (default: 11)
  theme_bw(base_size = 13) +
    theme(
      # Remove the minor grid lines (those between the axis ticks)
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      # Center the title (default: left-aligned)
      plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5)
    )
)
```
:::


All plots that you make after running this code will use this theme,
including all plots in the rest of this page. Things to keep in mind:

- The default theme only lasts for the current R session.
  So, in a Quarto document, put `theme_set()` in a chunk near the top,
  right after loading your packages.
- You can still change the theme for individual plots,
  by adding `theme()` or another theme to them.
- To go back to _ggplot2_'s default theme, run `theme_set(theme_gray())`.

## Adjusting axes with `scale_` functions

Each aesthetic, including the x and y position, has a **scale**,
which controls how data values are translated into, e.g., positions along an axis or colors.
_ggplot2_ picks defaults for each aesthetic,
but you can make changes with a `scale_<aesthetic>_<type>()` function.
You already saw two of these in week 13:
`scale_color_manual()` and `scale_y_log10()`.

Let's start with a scatter plot of the number of detected genes versus library size,
which we'll improve with some scale functions.
Because both axes show continuous variables,
the functions to use are `scale_x_continuous()` and `scale_y_continuous()`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sample_stats |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lib_size_M, y = n_detected)) +
  geom_point()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


### Number formatting with `labels`

Large numbers like the ones on the y-axis are easier to read with thousand separators.
You can add these with the `label_comma()` function from the _scales_ package,
which was installed along with the _tidyverse_:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sample_stats |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lib_size_M, y = n_detected)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma())
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The `scales::` prefix lets you use a function from a package without loading it.
The _scales_ package has similar functions for other formats,
like `label_percent()` for percentages.

### Starting an axis at 0 with `limits`

By default, each axis only covers the range of the data.
So, in the plot above, the y-axis starts just below 14,000,
which makes the differences in the number of detected genes look large.
To make an axis start at 0, use `limits = c(0, NA)`,
where `NA` means "keep the default" for the upper limit:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sample_stats |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lib_size_M, y = n_detected)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(), limits = c(0, NA))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Now you can see that the number of detected genes varies little between samples,
compared to the library size.

::: {.callout-warning}
#### Limits remove data
Limits that are narrower than the range of your data
**remove** the data outside the limits from the plot,
with a "Removed rows" warning that is easy to miss.
To zoom in on part of a plot without removing any data,
use `coord_cartesian()` instead, such as `coord_cartesian(xlim = c(15, 25))`.
:::

### Tick marks with `breaks`

With `breaks`, you choose where the tick marks and their labels go.
For example, to have a tick mark every 5 million reads along the x-axis:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sample_stats |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lib_size_M, y = n_detected)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, NA), breaks = c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(), limits = c(0, NA))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


### Removing the gap below bars with `expand`

Even with a limit of 0, there is a small gap between the axis and the start of the data,
because _ggplot2_ by default expands each axis by 5% on both sides.
This gap is especially noticeable in bar graphs --- for example:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sample_stats |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lib_size_M, y = sample_id)) +
  geom_col() +
  # Remove the horizontal grid lines (more on theme() below):
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


To remove the gap at the start of the axis, use the `expand` argument with the `expansion()` function.
Its `mult` argument takes the expansion at the lower and upper end of the axis,
as proportions of the axis range.
Here, we'll keep the default 5% at the upper end, so the longest bar doesn't touch the edge of the plot:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sample_stats |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lib_size_M, y = sample_id)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


All of these arguments also work in the other axis scale functions,
like `scale_x_log10()` and `scale_y_log10()`,
and you'll use them in many plots below.

## Bar graphs with `geom_bar()`

In the lecture,
you made [bar graphs with `geom_col()`](/week13/w13b_data-viz.qmd#bar-graphs-with-geom_col),
where the bar heights are **values that are already in your data**.
A closely related geom is `geom_bar()`,
which instead **counts the number of rows** for each category.

For example, to plot the number of genes without any reads in each sample,
you can keep only the rows of `counts_long` with a count of 0,
and then use `geom_bar()`, which counts the remaining rows for each sample:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
counts_long |>
  filter(count == 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = sample_id)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_comma(),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))
  ) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


A notable feature of `geom_bar()` is that you don't need to specify both an x and
a y variable: you specify **only** the variable to count,
and _ggplot2_ computes the other axis for you.
Here, we put `sample_id` on the y-axis, which gives **horizontal bars**,
so the sample ID labels don't overlap.

<details class="details-quiz"><summary>What would this plot look like if you removed the `filter()` line?</summary>

All bars would have the same length:
without the filter, `counts_long` has one row for every gene in every sample,
so `geom_bar()` would count the total number of genes (18,855) for each sample.

</details>

So, in short:

- Use `geom_col()` when your data frame already contains the numbers to plot.
- Use `geom_bar()` when you want to plot the number of rows per category.

## Histograms

To see the **distribution** of a single numeric variable,
use a histogram with `geom_histogram()`.
It counts rows like `geom_bar()`,
but first groups the values of a continuous variable into "**bins**".

Let's look at the distribution of gene counts in sample `S63`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
counts_long |>
  filter(sample_id == "S63") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = count)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "steelblue", color = "grey20") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_comma(),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma())
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

``` regular-r-output
`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.
```


:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The message tells you that `geom_histogram()` used its default of 30 bins,
and that you can pick a better bin width yourself, which we'll do below.

This plot is not very informative: because a few genes have extremely high counts,
nearly all genes end up in the first bin. Let's make a few changes to improve it:

- For counts like these, a **log scale** works much better (`log10(count)`).
- Because `log10(0)` is `-Inf` (negative infinity),
  we can **add 1** to the counts first (`log10(count + 1)`),
  so that zero-count genes are not dropped from the plot.
- We'll set the width of the bins with `binwidth` to get a more fine-grained
  view of the distribution.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
counts_long |>
  filter(sample_id == "S63") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = log10(count + 1))) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1, fill = "steelblue", color = "grey20") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_comma(),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The bar at 0 shows the genes without any reads,
and most other genes have between 10 (`1` on the x-axis) and 10,000 (`4` on the x-axis) reads.

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise: Histograms

1. Try a much smaller and a much larger `binwidth`, like 0.01 and 1.
   What happens to the histogram?

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_</summary>


   ::: {.cell}
   
   ```{.r .cell-code}
   counts_long |>
     filter(sample_id == "S63") |>
     ggplot(aes(x = log10(count + 1))) +
     geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.01)
   ```
   
   ::: {.cell-output-display}
   ![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=672}
   :::
   
   ```{.r .cell-code}
   counts_long |>
     filter(sample_id == "S63") |>
     ggplot(aes(x = log10(count + 1))) +
     geom_histogram(binwidth = 1)
   ```
   
   ::: {.cell-output-display}
   ![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-2.png){width=672}
   :::
   :::


   With very narrow bins, the histogram gets spiky and noisy,
   while with very wide bins, you lose the shape of the distribution.
   There is no single correct binwidth, so it's worth trying a few.

   </details>

2. Plot the histogram (with `binwidth = 0.1`) for both sample `S63` and sample `S77`,
   which has the smallest library,
   and fill the bars by `sample_id`.
   How are the bars of the two samples arranged?

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_</summary>


   ::: {.cell}
   
   ```{.r .cell-code}
   counts_long |>
     # Keep the rows for either of the two samples:
     filter(sample_id %in% c("S63", "S77")) |>
     ggplot(aes(x = log10(count + 1), fill = sample_id)) +
     geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1)
   ```
   
   ::: {.cell-output-display}
   ![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=672}
   :::
   :::


   The bars of the two samples are stacked on top of each other,
   so the total height of each bar is the count across both samples.

   </details>

3. Now, add `position = "identity"` and `alpha = 0.5` inside `geom_histogram()`.
   What does each of these two options do?
   And how do the distributions of the two samples differ?

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_</summary>


   ::: {.cell}
   
   ```{.r .cell-code}
   counts_long |>
     filter(sample_id %in% c("S63", "S77")) |>
     ggplot(aes(x = log10(count + 1), fill = sample_id)) +
     geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1, position = "identity", alpha = 0.5)
   ```
   
   ::: {.cell-output-display}
   ![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=672}
   :::
   :::


   - `position = "identity"` stops the stacking:
     each sample's bars start at zero, so they overlap.
   - `alpha = 0.5` makes the bars semi-transparent
     (`alpha` ranges from 0, fully transparent, to 1, opaque),
     so you can see the overlapping bars.

   The distribution of `S77` is shifted to the left,
   and it has more genes with zero counts:
   with fewer reads in total, each gene tends to get fewer reads.

   </details>
:::

## Faceting

When you map many variables in a single plot, it can get cluttered.
An alternative is **faceting**: creating multiple panels ("facets"),
one for each value of a categorical variable.
There are two faceting functions:

- `facet_wrap()` --- Facet by a single categorical variable,
  with the panels "wrapped" into a rectangular layout.
- `facet_grid()` --- Facet by one or two categorical variables,
  with the panels laid out in a grid of rows and columns.

For example, to make the count histogram from above for every sample:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
counts_long |>
  ggplot(aes(x = log10(count + 1))) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(vars(sample_id))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The distributions are similar for all samples,
as you would expect, because most genes are expressed at similar levels in all samples.
The clearest exception is `S77`, whose distribution is shifted to the left,
as you saw in the exercise above, because of its small library.

Faceting works with any type of plot.
For example, to make a box plot of the counts of a chymotrypsin gene (a digestive enzyme),
`LOC120423767`, for each treatment, with one panel per time point:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
counts_long |>
  filter(gene_id == "LOC120423767") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = treatment, y = count)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  facet_wrap(vars(time)) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


This gene is highly expressed at 24 hpi,
except in the _relictum_ samples,
and expression is low in all treatments at 10 dpi.

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise: Faceting

Make a box plot of the counts of two genes:
the chymotrypsin gene from above, and the cathepsin gene `LOC120419697`.
Use `facet_grid()` with the genes in rows and the time points in columns.
Hint: check the `scales` argument in the help for `facet_grid()`.
How do the expression patterns of the two genes differ?

<details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_</summary>


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
counts_long |>
  filter(gene_id %in% c("LOC120423767", "LOC120419697")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = treatment, y = count)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(gene_id), cols = vars(time), scales = "free_y")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


`scales = "free_y"` lets each row of panels have its own y-axis range,
which is needed here because the cathepsin gene has far higher counts.

The cathepsin gene is very highly expressed at 24 hpi in all treatments,
and barely expressed at 10 dpi,
while the chymotrypsin gene is barely expressed in the _relictum_ samples at 24 hpi.

</details>
:::

## Customizing themes

A theme controls the look of all parts of a plot that don't show your data,
like the text, the background, the grid lines, and the legend.
Complete themes like `theme_bw()` set all of these at once,
while the `theme()` function lets you change **individual parts**.

You've already used `theme()` on this page to remove grid lines,
and the [week 13 lecture](../week13/w13b_data-viz.qmd#adding-labels-and-a-theme)
also used it to move the legend:

```r
# [Other plotting code] +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

### How `theme()` works

Each argument name in `theme()` is a plot element,
like `axis.title` or `legend.position`,
and its value specifies the look of that element.
For most elements, you use one of four `element_*()` functions:

| Function          | Use for                                  | Common arguments                          |
|-------------------|------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| `element_text()`  | Text, like titles and axis labels        | `size`, `face`, `color`, `angle`, `hjust` |
| `element_line()`  | Lines, like grid lines and axis lines    | `color`, `linewidth`, `linetype`          |
| `element_rect()`  | Rectangles, like backgrounds and borders | `fill`, `color`                           |
| `element_blank()` | Any element: removes it                  | (None)                                    |

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

(A few elements take a plain value instead, like `legend.position = "top"`.)

Element names go from general to specific,
and more specific elements "inherit from" more general ones^[
  That is, if you set something for a general element, like `axis.title`, it will also apply to the more specific elements, like `axis.title.x` and `axis.title.y`, unless you set those specifically.
]. For example:

- `text` changes all text in the plot
- `axis.title` changes the titles of both axes
- `axis.title.x` changes only the x-axis title

`theme()` only changes the elements you specify,
and keeps everything else from the current theme,
such as the default theme that you set with `theme_set()`.

### Grid lines (and backgrounds)

In addition to removing minor grid lines, which tend to make the plot look busy,
it often makes sense to keep the major grid lines only for the axis that is
most important to read.

For example, in a box plot with treatments on the x-axis,
the vertical grid lines don't add much --- let's remove them:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sample_stats |>
  ggplot(aes(x = treatment, y = lib_size_M)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Getting fancy with grid lines and backgrounds _(Click to expand)_

You can use `element_rect()` to change the background and borders of the plot.
Here, we'll make the horizontal grid lines dashed,
give the plot panel a light gray background, and remove the panel border:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sample_stats |>
  ggplot(aes(x = treatment, y = lib_size_M)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "grey70", linetype = "dashed"),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "grey95"),
    panel.border = element_blank()
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


:::

### Text

To change the size of the plot title and the axis text,
and to make the title bold:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sample_stats |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lib_size_M, y = n_detected, color = treatment)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Detected genes vs. library size") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold"),
    # axis.title = the axis labels; axis.text = the numbers along the axes
    axis.title = element_text(size = 15),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 13)
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


(The title is still centered,
because the default theme you set earlier contains `hjust = 0.5` for `plot.title`,
and `theme()` only changed the size and font face.)

### Rotating axis labels

When you have many categories on the x-axis, like sample IDs,
the labels can overlap:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sample_stats |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sample_id, y = lib_size_M, fill = treatment)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


To fix this, rotate the labels with the `angle` argument of `element_text()`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sample_stats |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sample_id, y = lib_size_M, fill = treatment)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    # hjust = 1 lines up the end of each label with its tick mark,
    # and vjust = 0.5 centers each label on its tick mark
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5)
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-26-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Alternatively, put the categories on the y-axis,
as in the [`geom_bar()` example](#bar-graphs-with-geom_bar) above:
with horizontal bars, the labels don't need to be rotated and are easier to read.

### The legend

By default, _ggplot2_ puts the legend on the right side of the plot.
You can move it with the `legend.position` argument of `theme()`,
with possible values `"top"`, `"bottom"`, `"left"`, `"right"`,
or `"none"` (which removes the legend).

The legend title is the name of the mapped variable, here `treatment`.
To change it, use `labs()` with the name of the aesthetic,
like `labs(color = "Treatment")`, or `labs(fill = ...)` for a fill legend.

For example, to put the legend above the plot and capitalize its title:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sample_stats |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lib_size_M, y = n_detected, color = treatment)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(color = "Treatment") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
For all theme elements that you can change, see the
[`theme()` documentation {{< fa external-link >}}](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/theme.html){target="_blank"}.
:::

## Color palettes

You may not always be happy with the default colors that _ggplot2_ chooses for your plots.
You can pick your own colors with `scale_color_manual()`,
but that can be tedious if you have many categories.
Instead, you can use ready-made **color palettes**, which several packages provide.

### A starting plot

Before we look at color palettes, let's make one change to our earlier scatter plot:
we'll **fill** the points while keeping the outline dark,
which tends to look better and makes it easier to distinguish overlapping points.

To do this, we use the `shape` aesthetic to choose a point shape with a fill color,
like shape 21 (see [this overview of point shapes {{< fa external-link >}}](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/articles/ggplot2-specs.html#point){target="_blank"}):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sample_stats |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lib_size_M, y = n_detected, fill = treatment)) +
  geom_point(size = 4, shape = 21, color = "black") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma())
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-28-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


### RColorBrewer and ggsci

One example is the _RColorBrewer_ package
that you [installed in week 12](../week12/w12b_r-basics.qmd#r-packages),
which has palettes like `Dark2`:

![](/img/color_palette.png){width="65%" fig-align="center" .no-border .lightbox fig-alt="Color palette from the RColorBrewer package, showing 8 colors in the Dark2 palette."}

To use one of these palettes, use _ggplot2_'s `scale_fill_brewer()` function
(you don't need to load _RColorBrewer_ for this).
For example, to use the `Dark2` palette for a scatter plot:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sample_stats |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lib_size_M, y = n_detected, fill = treatment)) +
  geom_point(size = 4, shape = 21, color = "black") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Dark2")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-29-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Another popular option is the
[_ggsci_ package {{< fa external-link >}}](https://nanx.me/ggsci/){target="_blank"},
which has palettes based on the colors used by scientific journals,
such as `scale_fill_npg()` for _Nature_ and `scale_fill_lancet()` for _The Lancet_.

Install and then load the package:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
install.packages("ggsci")
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(ggsci)
```
:::


Use its `scale_fill_npg()` function:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sample_stats |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lib_size_M, y = n_detected, fill = treatment)) +
  geom_point(size = 4, shape = 21, color = "black") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_fill_npg()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-32-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


### viridis palettes

Finally, _ggplot2_ itself includes the **viridis** palettes,
whose colors stay distinguishable for colorblind readers and when printed in grayscale.
Use `scale_color_viridis_d()` / `scale_fill_viridis_d()` for categorical variables
like `treatment`,
and `scale_color_viridis_c()` / `scale_fill_viridis_c()` for continuous variables.

Viridis is especially popular for **heatmaps**,
which show a continuous variable with `fill` colors.
For example, to make a heatmap of the counts of the 10 most highly expressed genes
with `geom_tile()`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Get the 10 genes with the highest mean count:
top_genes <- counts_long |>
  summarize(mean_count = mean(count), .by = gene_id) |>
  # slice_max() will return the rows with the highest values of mean_count:
  slice_max(mean_count, n = 10)

counts_long |>
  filter(gene_id %in% top_genes$gene_id) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sample_id, y = gene_id, fill = log10(count))) +
  geom_tile(color = "grey50") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-33-1.png){width=768}
:::
:::


## Combining plots into one figure

### The _patchwork_ package

Figures in papers often combine different plots as panels A, B, and so on.
Faceting can't do this, because all facets show the same type of plot and variables.
Instead, you can use the [_patchwork_ {{< fa external-link >}}](https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com/){target="_blank"} package,
which is not part of the _tidyverse_.
Install and then load the package:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
install.packages("patchwork")
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(patchwork)
```
:::


First, save each plot as an object:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
scatter_plot <- sample_stats |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lib_size_M, y = n_detected, color = treatment)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

box_plot <- counts_long |>
  filter(gene_id == "LOC120423767") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = treatment, y = count)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(vars(time))
```
:::


Then, combine them with `|` to put plots side by side
(or `/` to put them on top of each other),
and add panel labels with `plot_annotation()`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
(scatter_plot | box_plot) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-plotting_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-37-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


The result is a single plot object,
which you can save to a file with `ggsave()` like any other plot.

### Getting Claude's help

Getting a multi-panel figure ready for a journal often takes a lot of small tweaks,
which you can ask Claude to help with, for example:

> ***Combine scatter_plot and box_plot into one figure with panels labeled A and B,***
> ***color the boxes by treatment like the points in the scatter plot,***
> ***and save it as a PDF that is 180 mm wide, the full page width in many journals.***

Then, check the `width`, `height`, and `units` arguments in Claude's `ggsave()` call,
and open the PDF to check that all text is still readable at that size.
